steps.title: Momentum: how hard something is to stop
steps.body:
A lorry rolling at walking pace and a tennis ball at 100 mph are both hard to stop, for different reasons. **Momentum** puts the two reasons into one number:

$$p = m v$$

$p$ is momentum in kilogram metres per second (kg m/s), $m$ is mass in kg, $v$ is velocity in m/s.

Double the mass and you double the momentum. Double the speed and you double it again. Something at rest has none at all, however heavy it is.

This equation is **not** on the AQA equation sheet. You have to know it.

visuals.alt: A card showing momentum equals mass times velocity, with units kg m/s, kg and m/s

check.prompt: A 2 kg trolley moves at 3 m/s. Calculate its momentum.

steps.title: Momentum has a direction
steps.body:
Momentum uses **velocity**, not speed, and velocity has a direction. So momentum does too.

Two cars of the same mass at the same speed, one heading north and one heading south, have momenta of the same size in **opposite** directions. Add them together and you get zero.

In a calculation you handle this with signs. Pick a direction to call positive, usually the way the first object is moving, and give anything moving the other way a **negative** velocity. Keep the sign all the way through; it is where most of the marks in the harder questions live.

steps.text: Car A: 1000 kg moving east at 10 m/s. Take east as positive: $p = 1000 \times 10 = +10\,000$ kg m/s
Car B: 1000 kg moving west at 10 m/s: $v = -10$ m/s, so $p = 1000 \times (-10) = -10\,000$ kg m/s

steps.note: Two large momenta can add to nothing

check.prompt: A 4 kg object moves left at 5 m/s. Taking right as positive, what is its momentum?
check.solution: Left is the negative direction, so $v = -5$ m/s and $p = 4 \times (-5) = -20$ kg m/s. The size is 20; the sign carries the direction.

steps.title: Rearranging for mass or velocity
steps.body:
Most questions give you two of $p$, $m$ and $v$ and ask for the third. Cover up the one you want:

$$v = \dfrac{p}{m} \qquad m = \dfrac{p}{v}$$

Write the rearranged equation down before you put numbers in. In a three-mark question the rearrangement is usually a mark on its own.

visuals.problem: A skater has momentum 150 kg m/s and mass 60 kg. Find her velocity.

check.prompt: An object with momentum 24 kg m/s moves at 8 m/s. Calculate its mass.

steps.title: Conservation of momentum
steps.body:
Higher tier only. In a **closed system**, one with no outside forces acting, the total momentum **before** an event equals the total momentum **after** it. This is the **principle of conservation of momentum**, and it holds for collisions, explosions, and anything in between.

A collision question is always the same three lines:

1. Total momentum before, adding each object's $m v$ with its sign.
2. Total momentum after, with the unknown velocity as a letter.
3. Set them equal and solve.

If two objects **stick together**, treat them as one object afterwards with the masses added.

visuals.alt: Before: a 2 kg block A moving right at 3 m/s towards a 1 kg block B at rest. After: the two stuck together as 3 kg moving right at 2 m/s

visuals.problem: A 4 kg trolley moving at 3 m/s catches up a 2 kg trolley moving the same way at 1.5 m/s. They couple together. Find their velocity.

steps.text: Take the direction of motion as positive
steps.note: both trolleys move the same way, so both velocities are positive
coupled means one object with the masses added
positive, so still in the original direction

check.prompt: A 2 kg block moving at 3 m/s hits a 1 kg block at rest and they stick together. Calculate their velocity afterwards.
check.solution: Before: $2 \times 3 + 1 \times 0 = 6$ kg m/s. After: $3 v$. So $3 v = 6$ and $v = 2$ m/s.

steps.title: Explosions and recoil
steps.body:
An **explosion** is a collision run backwards: one object at rest becomes two moving apart. The total momentum before is **zero**, so the total after must be zero as well. The two pieces have equal and opposite momentum.

That is why a gun recoils. The bullet is light and fast, the gun is heavy and slow, and $m v$ comes out the same for both.

visuals.alt: Before: a gun with its bullet at rest. After: the 0.05 kg bullet moving right at 400 m/s and the 2 kg gun recoiling left at 10 m/s

visuals.problem: A 2 kg gun fires a 0.05 kg bullet at 400 m/s. Find the recoil speed.

steps.text: Total momentum before $= 0$, because nothing is moving
Bullet after: $0.05 \times 400 = 20$ kg m/s, call it positive
Gun after must be $-20$ kg m/s so the total is still zero

steps.note: The minus sign is the recoil direction; the speed is 10 m/s

check.prompt: A 3 kg cannon on a frictionless surface fires a 0.1 kg ball at 60 m/s. Calculate the cannon's recoil speed.
check.solution: Ball: $0.1 \times 60 = 6$ kg m/s. The cannon needs 6 kg m/s the other way: $3 v = 6$, $v = 2$ m/s.

steps.title: Force is the rate of change of momentum
steps.body:
Higher tier, Physics only. To change something's momentum you need a force, and the faster you want to change it, the bigger the force:

$$F = \dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{m \Delta v}{\Delta t}$$

$F$ is force in N, $\Delta p$ is the change in momentum in kg m/s, $\Delta t$ is the time the change takes in s. The triangle $\Delta$ means *change in*.

This is Newton's second law in its original form. Rearranged, $F = m \times \dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = m a$, which is the version you met first.

It is on the equation sheet, but you need to recognise when a question is asking for it: any time you see a mass, a change in speed, and a **time**.

equations.name: Force from a change in momentum

visuals.alt: A card with momentum equals m v, and force equals change in momentum divided by time

visuals.problem: A 1200 kg car slows from 25 m/s to 10 m/s in 6 s. Find the average braking force.

steps.note: same direction throughout, so a plain subtraction
change in momentum, not the momentum at either end
check with $F = m a$: $a = 15 \div 6 = 2.5$ m/s², and $1200 \times 2.5 = 3000$ N

check.prompt: A 0.2 kg ball's velocity changes by 30 m/s in 0.05 s. Calculate the average force on it.

steps.title: Why safety features work
steps.body:
In a crash, a passenger's momentum has to fall to zero. That change in momentum is fixed: it is their mass times their speed, and no gadget can alter it.

What a safety feature **can** alter is the **time** the change takes. Since $F = \Delta p / \Delta t$, a longer time means a smaller force, and a smaller force means less injury.

- **Crumple zones** fold up, so the car takes longer to stop.
- **Seat belts** stretch slightly, so the passenger slows over a longer time than hitting the dashboard.
- **Air bags** inflate then deflate as you press into them, stretching the time out and spreading the force over a larger area.
- **Crash mats**, **cycle helmets** and the bent knees of a gymnast landing all do the same job.

The examiner's phrase is *increases the time taken for the change in momentum, so reduces the force*. Write it in that order.

visuals.problem: Same change in momentum, different times

steps.text: A 70 kg passenger at 13 m/s: $\Delta p = 70 \times 13 = 910$ kg m/s, whatever happens next
Stopped by the dashboard in 0.1 s: $F = 910 \div 0.1 = 9100$ N
Stopped by a seat belt in 1.5 s: $F = 910 \div 1.5 \approx 607$ N
Fifteen times longer, fifteen times less force
steps.note: The momentum change never moved; only the time did

check.prompt: Which sentence best explains why an air bag reduces injury?
check.solution: The momentum change is fixed. The air bag makes it take longer, and $F = \Delta p / \Delta t$ means a longer time gives a smaller force. It does spread the force over a larger area too, but the main effect is the time.

markScheme.description: increases the time, so reduces the force

options: It increases the time taken for the passenger's momentum to change, so the force is smaller
It reduces the passenger's momentum before the crash
It increases the force on the passenger but spreads it out
It stops the passenger's momentum changing

steps.title: Your turn: momentum against velocity
steps.body:
The slider sets the velocity of a 1500 kg car. Read its momentum off the graph.

It is a straight line through the origin because $p = m v$ with $m$ fixed: the gradient of the line **is** the mass. Check: at 20 m/s the momentum should be $1500 \times 20 = 30\,000$ kg m/s.

visuals.fallback: A straight line from the origin with gradient 1500: 15 000 kg m/s at 10 m/s, 30 000 kg m/s at 20 m/s, 45 000 kg m/s at 30 m/s.

check.prompt: Using $p = m v$, what is the momentum of the 1500 kg car at 30 m/s?

steps.title: Grade 9: when the velocity reverses
steps.body:
The question that separates grade 9 from grade 7 is a ball bouncing off a wall.

A 0.06 kg ball hits a wall at 20 m/s and comes back at 15 m/s. What is its change in momentum?

The trap is $0.06 \times (20 - 15) = 0.3$. That is wrong, because the velocity has **reversed**. Take *towards the wall* as positive: before, $p = 0.06 \times 20 = 1.2$; after, $p = 0.06 \times (-15) = -0.9$. The change is $-0.9 - 1.2 = -2.1$ kg m/s: a magnitude of $2.1$, seven times the trap answer.

The same care applies to head-on collisions. One object gets a negative velocity **before** you add the momenta, and the answer's sign tells you which way the wreckage moves.

The other grade 9 habit is spotting that a question in a strange setting is one you know. A satellite firing a thruster is a gun firing a bullet. Two skaters pushing apart is an explosion. Total momentum zero before, so equal and opposite after.

visuals.alt: Before: a 3 kg block A moving right at 4 m/s and a 1 kg block B moving left at 2 m/s towards it. After: the two stuck together as 4 kg moving right at 2.5 m/s

visuals.problem: Head-on: 3 kg at 4 m/s right meets 1 kg at 2 m/s left, and they stick

steps.text: Right is positive. B's velocity is $-2$ m/s
$4v = 10$, so $v = 2.5$ m/s, positive, so to the right
steps.note: Adding $12 + 2 = 14$ instead is the mark most people drop

check.prompt: A 0.5 kg ball hits the floor at 8 m/s and bounces up at 6 m/s. Calculate the magnitude of its change in momentum.
check.skill: change in momentum with a reversal
check.solution: Down positive: before $0.5 \times 8 = 4$, after $0.5 \times (-6) = -3$. Change $= -3 - 4 = -7$, magnitude 7 kg m/s. Not $0.5 \times 2 = 1$.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Momentum** $p = m v$, in kg m/s. Not on the equation sheet; learn it.
- **It has direction.** Choose a positive direction and give the other way a minus sign. Keep the sign through the whole calculation.
- **Conservation of momentum**: in a closed system, total momentum before $=$ total momentum after. Three lines: before, after with an unknown, set equal.
- **Stuck together** afterwards means one object with the masses added.
- **Explosions and recoil** start from zero total momentum, so the pieces have equal and opposite momentum.
- **Force** $F = \dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$. A bigger change, or a shorter time, needs a bigger force.
- **Safety features** increase the time taken for the momentum to change, which reduces the force. Say it in that order.
- **Velocity reversing** means the change in momentum is $m(v + u)$ in size, not $m(v - u)$.

Conservation

questions.prompt: A car of mass 1200 kg travels at 20 m/s. Calculate its momentum.
What is the unit of momentum?
questions.solution: Momentum is mass times velocity, so its unit is kilograms times metres per second: kg m/s.

questions.prompt: A ball of mass 0.5 kg moves at 12 m/s. Calculate its momentum.
Which of these has zero momentum?
questions.solution: Momentum is $m v$. A parked lorry has a large mass but its velocity is zero, so its momentum is zero. Everything moving, however slowly or however light, has some.
options: A lorry parked at the roadside
A bullet just after it is fired

questions.prompt: An object has momentum 30 kg m/s and mass 6 kg. Calculate its velocity.
A trolley moving at 9 m/s has momentum 45 kg m/s. Calculate its mass.
A 2 kg trolley moving at 4 m/s collides with a stationary 2 kg trolley. They stick together. Calculate their velocity after the collision.
questions.solution: Momentum before $= 2 \times 4 + 2 \times 0 = 8$ kg m/s. After, the combined mass is 4 kg and momentum is conserved: $4 v = 8$, so $v = 2$ m/s.

questions.prompt: A cricket ball of mass 0.16 kg is struck so that its velocity changes by 25 m/s in 0.02 s. Calculate the average force on the ball.
questions.solution: Change in momentum $= 0.16 \times 25 = 4$ kg m/s. $F = \dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{4}{0.02} = 200$ N.

questions.prompt: A car's crumple zone folds up in a crash. Why does this reduce the force on the passengers?
questions.solution: The change in momentum is fixed by the car's mass and speed. $F = \dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$, so making the collision take longer makes the force smaller. The crumple zone does nothing to the mass or the momentum; it buys time.

markScheme.description: increases the time for the momentum change

options: It increases the time taken for the momentum to change
It reduces the mass of the car
It reduces the time taken for the momentum to change

questions.prompt: A gun of mass 2 kg fires a bullet of mass 0.05 kg at 400 m/s. Calculate the recoil speed of the gun.
questions.solution: Before firing, total momentum is 0. After, the bullet has $0.05 \times 400 = 20$ kg m/s forwards, so the gun must have 20 kg m/s backwards: $2 v = 20$, $v = 10$ m/s.

markScheme.description: gun momentum equal and opposite: $2 v = 20$

questions.prompt: A 3 kg cart moving at 4 m/s to the right collides head-on with a 1 kg cart moving at 2 m/s to the left. They stick together. Calculate their velocity after the collision, taking right as positive.
questions.solution: Take right as positive, so the 1 kg cart's velocity is $-2$ m/s. Momentum before $= 3 \times 4 + 1 \times (-2) = 12 - 2 = 10$ kg m/s. Combined mass 4 kg: $4 v = 10$, $v = 2.5$ m/s, to the right.

markScheme.description: left-moving cart given a negative velocity

questions.prompt: A car of mass 800 kg moving at 15 m/s hits a stationary van of mass 1200 kg. After the collision the car continues in the same direction at 3 m/s. Calculate the velocity of the van after the collision.
questions.skill: conservation with both bodies moving after
questions.solution: Momentum before $= 800 \times 15 = 12\,000$ kg m/s. After: $800 \times 3 + 1200 v = 2400 + 1200 v$. Conservation: $2400 + 1200 v = 12\,000$, so $1200 v = 9600$ and $v = 8$ m/s.

questions.prompt: A tennis ball of mass 0.06 kg hits a wall at 20 m/s and rebounds at 15 m/s. Calculate the magnitude of the change in momentum of the ball.
questions.skill: change in momentum with a reversal
questions.solution: Velocity reverses, so the change is not $20 - 15$. Take towards the wall as positive: before $= 0.06 \times 20 = 1.2$ kg m/s; after $= 0.06 \times (-15) = -0.9$ kg m/s. Change $= -0.9 - 1.2 = -2.1$, so the magnitude is $2.1$ kg m/s.

markScheme.description: rebound velocity given the opposite sign

questions.prompt: A golf ball of mass 0.045 kg is struck from rest and leaves the club at 50 m/s. The club is in contact with the ball for 0.0005 s. Calculate the average force exerted by the club.
questions.solution: $\Delta p = 0.045 \times 50 = 2.25$ kg m/s. $F = \dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{2.25}{0.0005} = 4500$ N. A force that large is fine for a tiny fraction of a second.

questions.prompt: Two trolleys are held together with a compressed spring between them. When released, the 0.5 kg trolley moves off at 6 m/s. Calculate the speed of the 1.5 kg trolley.
questions.solution: Before release the total momentum is zero, so afterwards the two momenta are equal and opposite. $0.5 \times 6 = 3$ kg m/s one way means $1.5 \times v = 3$ the other way, so $v = 2$ m/s.

questions.prompt: A satellite of mass 4000 kg is at rest. It fires 10 kg of gas from a thruster at 800 m/s. Calculate the speed of the satellite after firing. Take the satellite's mass after firing to be 4000 kg.
questions.solution: This is the gun and bullet in space. Total momentum starts at zero. Gas: $10 \times 800 = 8000$ kg m/s one way. Satellite: $4000 v = 8000$ the other way, $v = 2$ m/s.

questions.prompt: A passenger of mass 70 kg is travelling at 13 m/s when the car stops suddenly in a crash. Without a seat belt, the passenger is stopped by the dashboard in 0.1 s. With a seat belt, the passenger is brought to rest in 1.5 s. Show that the seat belt reduces the average force on the passenger by more than 8000 N.
questions.solution: Both forces use the same change in momentum, $70 \times 13 = 910$ kg m/s. Dashboard: $F = 910 \div 0.1 = 9100$ N. Seat belt: $F = 910 \div 1.5 \approx 607$ N. Difference $\approx 8493$ N, which is more than 8000 N, as required. The momentum change is the same in both cases; only the time differs.

markScheme.description: difference $\approx 8490$ N, greater than 8000 N, stated with the comparison

criteria.text: Change in momentum $= 70 \times 13 = 910$ kg m/s, calculated once and used for both cases
The difference, about 8490 N, is compared with 8000 N and the conclusion stated

questions.modelAnswer: $\Delta p = m \Delta v = 70 \times 13 = 910$ kg m/s in both cases. Without the belt: $F = \dfrac{910}{0.1} = 9100$ N. With the belt: $F = \dfrac{910}{1.5} = 607$ N (to 3 s.f.). The reduction is $9100 - 607 = 8493$ N, which is more than 8000 N, as required.

questions.prompt: Explain, using ideas about momentum, how seat belts and air bags reduce injuries to passengers in a car crash.
questions.solution: Level-marked. Level 3 links the fixed change in momentum, the increased stopping time, $F = \Delta p / \Delta t$, and the smaller force, for both features, and mentions that the belt stretches and the air bag deflates.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two relevant points, not linked
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a mostly correct account with some links between points
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a coherent, complete account with every step linked and correct physics terms

criteria.text: In a crash the car stops but the passenger keeps moving with their momentum, $m v$
The passenger's momentum must fall to zero; that change in momentum is fixed by their mass and speed
$F = \dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$: for a fixed change in momentum, a longer time means a smaller force
A seat belt stretches slightly, so the passenger slows over a longer time than hitting the dashboard
An air bag inflates and then deflates as the passenger presses into it, increasing the stopping time further and spreading the force over a larger area
A smaller force on the body means less injury; both features also stop the passenger hitting hard surfaces

questions.modelAnswer: When a car stops suddenly, the passenger keeps moving with momentum $m v$ until something stops them. Their momentum has to change to zero, and that change in momentum is fixed by their mass and speed. The force needed is $F = \Delta p / \Delta t$, so the only way to make the force smaller is to make the change take longer. A seat belt stretches a little, so the passenger is slowed over a longer time than they would be by hitting the dashboard. An air bag inflates and then deflates as the passenger presses into it, which increases the stopping time further and spreads the force over a larger area of the body. A smaller force means less injury.

examTechnique.body:
Momentum questions are worth between 2 and 6 marks and they are formulaic, which is good news: a collision is always *before, after, equate*, and a safety question is always *same change in momentum, longer time, smaller force*. $p = m v$ is not on the equation sheet, so it has to come from memory; $F = \Delta p / \Delta t$ is on the sheet but is easy to miss, because the question will not say *momentum* in it. If you see a mass, a change in speed and a time, that is the equation.

The marks people lose are nearly all about direction. Anything moving the other way gets a negative velocity, and a ball that bounces has a change in momentum of $m(u + v)$, not $m(u - v)$.
examinerErrors: Forgetting $p = m v$ under pressure. It is not on the sheet, and many students hunt for it there.
Adding the momenta of two objects moving towards each other. One of them is negative; the total is a difference, not a sum.
Working out the change in momentum of a bouncing ball as $m(u - v)$. The velocity reverses, so the change is $m(u + v)$ in size.
Using the mass of only one object after a stick-together collision. The combined object has both masses.
Explaining a crumple zone or air bag as *reducing the momentum* or *absorbing the force*. The momentum change is fixed; the feature increases the time, which reduces the force.
Giving a recoil velocity with no direction, or losing a mark for not saying it is opposite to the bullet. The sign in the working is the direction.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer sets a positive direction in the first line and gives every velocity its sign before writing a single momentum. In a collision it writes *before*, *after* and *equal* as three separate lines, with the unknown as a letter, and reads the direction of the answer off its sign. For a bounce it uses $m(u + v)$ without hesitating. In an explanation it says *increases the time taken for the momentum to change, so the force is smaller* in that order, and quotes $F = \Delta p / \Delta t$ to justify it. Given a satellite, a skater or a cannon, it recognises the gun and bullet underneath.
